name: Tolman-Bondi Inhomogeneous Dust Universe
description: A spherically symmetric but inhomogeneous dust solution generalizing FLRW to a density and an expansion that vary with position. It is widely used to model voids, structure formation, and inhomogeneous cosmologies.
history: The Tolman-Bondi solution is what the FLRW universe becomes when one stops insisting that the cosmos be the same everywhere. It keeps spherical symmetry and keeps the matter a pressureless dust, but lets the density and the rate of expansion vary with radius, so it can describe a universe with a lump in it, or a hole. Its name records three contributors in turn: Georges Lemaître wrote down the general spherically symmetric dust models in 1933 [lemaitre1933], Richard Tolman examined what inhomogeneity does to a cosmology the following year [tolman1934], and Hermann Bondi systematized the whole family in 1947, identifying the local energy as the parameter that fixes the geometry [bondi1947]. Hence Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi, or LTB. Andrzej Krasiński pointed out in 1997 that Tolman made no secret that the solution he discussed was Lemaître's, and proposed calling it the Lemaître-Tolman model [krasinski1997].¶The solution's charm is that it is exactly solvable despite being inhomogeneous, and the reason is a kind of independence: each concentric shell of dust evolves on its own, like a miniature FLRW universe with its own spatial curvature and its own clock, neighboring shells neither knowing nor caring what the others do. Set the radial profiles to constants and ordinary FLRW reappears; take a single uniform ball and match it to an exterior vacuum and one recovers the Oppenheimer-Snyder model of collapse [oppenheimersnyder1939, christodoulou1984]. W. B. Bonnor showed in 1974 that an open Robertson-Walker universe can grow from many initial states, since there are inhomogeneous models of this kind whose initial density is an arbitrary function of radius and which approach the Robertson-Walker form as time goes on [bonnor1974]. LTB is the connective tissue between the homogeneous cosmos and the collapsing star.¶P. Yodzis, H. J. Seifert, and H. Müller zum Hagen showed in 1973 that even the spherically symmetric collapse of dust can produce singularities not hidden inside black holes, where neighboring shells cross [yodzis1973]; such shell crossing singularities are gravitationally weak, places an observer would pass through undamaged [joshi2011]. Douglas Eardley and Larry Smarr, classifying Tolman-Bondi collapse by its causal structure in 1979, found naked singularities of a new type whenever the collapse is inhomogeneous enough [eardley1979]. Demetrios Christodoulou proved in 1984 that for an open set of initial density profiles the first singularity, at the center of the cloud, sends light rays out to infinity, infinitely redshifted [christodoulou1984]. Charles Hellaby and Kayll Lake derived in 1985 the conditions under which a Tolman model is free of shell crossings [hellaby1985]. R. P. A. C. Newman showed in 1986 that the central singularities are weak as well [newman1986, joshi2011], but Pankaj Joshi and I. H. Dwivedi found in 1993 that central naked singularities form in a wide class of these collapses, some of them strong curvature singularities that crush any volume to zero [joshi1993].¶That flexibility has made it the standard tool for inhomogeneity in general relativity. Lemaître had already used it to discuss how clusters of nebulae might form, an attempt within the exact theory that Krasiński judged at least twenty years ahead of its time [krasinski1997]. It models the growth of cosmic voids and the nonlinear formation of structure, and it has been pressed into more provocative service: a sufficiently large local void, described by an LTB metric, can mimic the dimming of distant supernovae that is usually read as cosmic acceleration, raising the question of whether some of what we attribute to dark energy is instead a sign that we sit near the center of an underdensity [tomita2001].¶Marie-Noëlle Célérier gave in 2000 an inhomogeneous model with no cosmological constant that reproduced the supernova data [celerier2000], and Håvard Alnes, Morad Amarzguioui, and Øyvind Grøn found in 2006 that an underdense bubble centered near the observer fits the supernova distances without dark energy [alnes2006]. Adam Moss, James Zibin, and Douglas Scott found void models in severe tension with the data in 2011: they predict too low a local Hubble rate and much less local structure than is observed [moss2011]. Pengjie Zhang and Albert Stebbins showed the same year that a void large enough to stand in for dark energy would raise a kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich signal far above the observed limits [zhang2011]. The proposal is constrained and largely disfavored [moss2011, zhang2011], but that it can even be posed is a measure of how much room inhomogeneity leaves in the field equations.

parameters.description: Areal radius, a length: the shell labelled $r$ has area $4\pi R^2$ at time $t$, and $R$ is an arbitrary positive function of both coordinates. The chart is regular where $\partial_r R > 0$, a shell crossing being where two shells meet and the density blows up without the geometry being singular. A printed $\partial_t$ is the derivative along the chart coordinate, $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$, so $\partial_t R$ and $\partial_r R$ are dimensionless and every further derivative carries one more inverse length.

Energy function, dimensionless, an arbitrary function of $r$ alone with $1 + 2E > 0$. It is the energy per unit mass of the shell labelled $r$ in units of $c^2$, so $E > 0$ is a shell with enough of it to escape, $E < 0$ one that must turn around and recollapse, and $E = 0$ the marginally bound case this entry does not specialise to. The same function fixes the curvature of the spatial slices, which is why the FLRW limit is $E = -kr^2/2$ with $R = a(t)r$. The prime is $E' = dE/dr$.
